summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1832. The age of consent is set at 14 under Criminal Code article 308bis, with a three-year close-in-age exemption.

Article 14(II) of the Constitution, in force since February 2009, prohibits and punishes discrimination based on gender identity.

The anti-discrimination statute defines discrimination to include gender identity and defines transphobia. It amended Penal Code article 281 to criminalize gender-identity-based discrimination. Dissemination of and incitement to such discrimination carry one to five years imprisonment. Since 2010, article 40bis aggravates penalties for crimes motivated by gender identity.

The Gender Identity Law was approved by the Chamber of Deputies on 19 May 2016 and by the Chamber of Senators on 20 May 2016, signed on 21 May 2016, and took effect on 1 August 2016. It permits persons over 18 to change name, sex and photograph on legal documents before the Civil Registry Service. The procedure is confidential and is to conclude within 15 days. It requires a psychological assessment of voluntary assumption. Sex reassignment surgery is not required. The change is reversible once only.

The reassigned sex is not accepted for purposes of marriage. In November 2017 the Supreme Court invalidated as unconstitutional a June 2017 instruction of the Supreme Electoral Tribunal that had directed recognition. An appeal was filed to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in May 2018. Article 63 of the Constitution limits marriage to heterosexual couples.

Same-sex couples may register free unions. The civil registry recognized such unions in December 2020. A ruling of the Plurinational Constitutional Court of 22 June 2022 obliging registration took effect on 20 March 2023. Regulations were modified by 21 July 2023 to apply the same requirements and time limits as for heterosexual couples. Fifteen couples had registered by January 2023 under Inter-American Court Advisory Opinion OC-24/17. The Inter-American Court had issued an advisory opinion on gender identity and same-sex family rights in January 2018.

Transgender persons may serve openly in the military under a 2013 Armed Forces announcement effective in 2015.

Protection in law has not ensured protection in practice. The Ombudsman reported that 64 LGBT persons were murdered in 2017, with only 14 cases investigated and none resulting in a sentence. The United States State Department in its 2011 report and other reporting describe societal discrimination against LGBT persons as not uncommon. A first virtual survey reported in December 2024 found extensive exclusion of LGBTI persons in Bolivia.

A 2017 ILGA poll specific to transgender attitudes found 64 percent agreed transgender persons should have the same rights, 63 percent believed they should be protected from employment discrimination, and 53 percent believed they should be allowed to change legal gender.
tangentialFactors:
A comparative study published in April 2024 found that the gender identity law was adopted despite low voter support through access by trans activists to ruling-party legislators. Contradictory heteronormative statutes were adopted in the same period because organized religion and LGBT activists were both party constituents.

Constitutional and criminal protections also extend to sexual orientation. Dissemination of and incitement to orientation-based discrimination carry one to five years imprisonment, and penalties for orientation-motivated crimes have been aggravated since 2010.

Press reporting in August 2014 described homosexuality as taboo in the armed forces. Gay soldiers reported discrimination and sanctions and gave testimony anonymously, while the TLGB collective and human rights activists demanded openness.
localsOnly:
Single persons may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. Same-sex couples in a free union are permitted to adopt under Article 84 of the Child and Adolescent Code.

Men who have sex with men have been permitted to donate blood since 10 July 2019 under amended Supreme Decree 24547, after a prior ban that classified homosexual and bisexual men as a high-risk group.

The first legal gender change under the 2016 law occurred on 1 August 2016 by activist Pamela Valenzuela.

The Constitution addresses violence in Article 15(II) and maternity in Article 45(V), while Title VIII of the Penal Code governs abortion.
outOfScopeNotes:
Rules on access to single-sex facilities, bathrooms and gendered accommodation were not sourced in the inventory and remain unresolved.

Entry, visa and border screening practice as applied to trans visitors, including treatment of foreign gender markers, was not sourced and remains unresolved.

Availability of gender-affirming care for short-term visitors, and any restriction affecting such care, was not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement trends after 2017, including investigation and sentencing outcomes for anti-trans violence beyond the 2017 Ombudsman figures, were not sourced and remain unresolved.
